gendered_labor.assessment: Men predominantly hunt, women predominantly gather, but gathered plant foods made up roughly two-thirds of caloric intake in Lee's Dobe-area data — women's labor was the larger single source of subsistence calories. Women are documented as owning/distributing meat as arrow-owners even without hunting themselves; female hunting occurs but is atypical (San-specific frequency not quantified in sources found). Women's central role in the healing dance (singers/clappers, and per Katz roughly 1/4 of healers) is a documented exception to a gathering-only framing.

sources.citation: Lee, Richard B. The !Kung San: Men, Women, and Work in a Foraging Society. Cambridge University Press, 1979.
sources.author: Richard B. Lee

political_inequality.assessment: DISPUTED on two axes. Gender axis: Lorna Marshall's Nyae Nyae fieldwork documents headmen with no formal privileges, achieved (not inherited) status, and consensus decision-making in which women's voices are documented as part of the process — but headmen in recorded cases appear predominantly male; no documented female headman among Ju/'hoansi specifically was located. Structural-historical axis (the "Kalahari Debate"): Lee/DeVore/Solway treated observed egalitarianism as reflecting a foraging-adapted social system; Edwin Wilmsen (Land Filled with Flies, University of Chicago Press, 1989) and James Denbow argued the San had been enmeshed in regional trade/political relationships with Bantu agropastoralists for up to ~1,500 years and that observed "egalitarianism" partly reflects a historically produced underclass position, not a pristine foraging baseline; Lee and Solway later co-acknowledged a long interaction history rather than pristine isolation.

sources.citation: Wilmsen, Edwin. Land Filled with Flies: A Political Economy of the Kalahari. University of Chicago Press, 1989.
sources.author: Edwin Wilmsen

sources.citation: Lee, Richard B., and Jacqueline Solway. "Foragers, Genuine or Spurious? Situating the Kalahari San in History." Current Anthropology.

legal_economic_status.assessment: Land/resource tenure organized around the n!ore (band territory) with k'"ausi (owners of the waterhole/resources), typically related elders with continuous tenure rights. Polly Wiessner's hxaro system (delayed-reciprocity gift exchange, PhD thesis 1977) documents both men and women holding and initiating individual exchange partnerships granting access to resources up to ~200km from home n!ore. Women's arrow-ownership functions as a documented, specific instance of female economic entitlement independent of the hunt.

sources.citation: Wiessner, Polly. "Hxaro: A Regional System of Reciprocity for Reducing Risk among the !Kung San." PhD thesis, 1977.
sources.author: Polly Wiessner

household_authority.assessment: Marjorie Shostak, Nisa: The Life and Words of a !Kung Woman (Harvard UP, 1981) documents bride-service of roughly 8-10 years (groom labors for bride's family before independent residence), often following marriages arranged for very young (sometimes pre-pubescent) girls to considerably older men — the age gap cited as part of the reason bride-service exists. Household labor is not rigidly gender-segregated: men participate in gathering and child discipline alongside wives. Nisa's own account documents a woman successfully resisting/fleeing an arranged marriage she did not consent to — real, documented female agency within the system.

sources.citation: Shostak, Marjorie. Nisa: The Life and Words of a !Kung Woman. Harvard University Press, 1981.
sources.author: Marjorie Shostak

gendered_legal_restrictions.assessment: Arranged, often significant-age-gap marriage for young/pre-pubescent girls to older partners is documented as a real, differentially-applied norm (girls, not boys, married young to older partners). Polygyny is documented but statistically concentrated among healers with strong reputations, suggesting it functions partly as a status marker tied to religious/healing prestige rather than general practice.

sources.citation: Shostak, Marjorie. Nisa: The Life and Words of a !Kung Woman. Harvard University Press, 1981.
sources.author: Marjorie Shostak

ideological_patriarchy.assessment: No basis found for either "straightforwardly subordinates women" or "straightforwardly gender-egalitarian" as a documented scholarly consensus for Ju/'hoansi cosmology specifically — report as genuinely unresolved rather than picking a side.

sources.citation: General absence of a dedicated study found in this research pass.

dimensions.notes: Distinct group/period from /Xam (gs_xam) — do not merge. Do not import Apollo 11 Cave rock-art age (~26,000-30,000 BP) or Khoe-San population-genetic divergence dates (Chan et al. 2019, Nature, itself disputed by other geneticists) into any claim about the age of this specific documented social/gender system — those are categorically different kinds of evidence.
